title: Pheidippides, the Runner of Marathon
subject: English
source: Written for english/y5 lesson 52 (Teacher's text: Pheidippides (lesson 49))
intro: Lesson 52. Read the text, then answer the questions. Use VIPERS: retrieve, use the vocabulary, infer, explain, summarise.

passage.title: Pheidippides, the Runner of Marathon
paras: In the summer of 490 BC, a huge Persian army landed on the beach at Marathon, a small town on the coast of Greece. The Persian king, Darius, wanted to punish the city of Athens, which had helped his enemies. The Athenians, who were badly outnumbered, needed help, and they needed it fast.

They turned to a man named Pheidippides. He was a hemerodromos, which means 'day-runner': a messenger trained to run long distances across the rocky Greek hills. His task was simple to say and terribly hard to do. He must run to Sparta to ask for help.

Sparta was about 240 kilometres away. According to the Greek historian Herodotus, Pheidippides reached it in around two days. He ran through the heat of the day and through the dark of the night. He did not stop to rest for longer than he had to, because he knew that the lives of everyone in Athens depended on his message.

When he arrived, the Spartans listened politely. They agreed to help, but there was a problem: they were in the middle of a religious festival and would not march until the moon was full. Exhausted, Pheidippides ran back with the disappointing news.
In the end, the Athenians fought at Marathon without the Spartans, and, to everyone's surprise, they won.

Hundreds of years later, a different story was told. In this legend, a runner raced the 40 kilometres from Marathon to Athens to announce the victory. He burst into the city, gasped 'We have won!' and collapsed. Historians are not sure this run ever happened; Herodotus, who wrote closest to the time, does not mention it.

True or not, the legend lived on. When the first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens in 1896, the organisers added a long-distance race that followed the route from Marathon to Athens. They named it after the town where the story began: the marathon.

questions.q: R: In which year did the Persian army land at Marathon?
questions.a: 490 BC

questions.q: R: Why did Pheidippides run to Sparta?
questions.a: To ask the Spartans for help.

questions.q: V: What does 'hemerodromos' mean?
questions.a: Day-runner: a messenger trained to run long distances.

questions.q: R: About how far was Sparta, and how long did it take him?
questions.a: About 240 kilometres, in around two days.

questions.q: I: How did Pheidippides feel when he set off? Give evidence.
questions.a: Determined: he 'did not stop to rest for longer than he had to', because the message mattered more than his tiredness.

questions.q: R: Why did the Spartans not march at once?
questions.a: They were in a religious festival and would not march until the moon was full.

questions.q: V: Find a word in paragraph 4 that means 'very tired'.
questions.a: Exhausted

questions.q: R: Who won the battle at Marathon?
questions.a: The Athenians.

questions.q: E: Why were the Athenians 'surprised' to win?
questions.a: They were badly outnumbered and fought without the Spartans.

questions.q: I: Why might historians doubt the run from Marathon to Athens?
questions.a: Herodotus, who wrote closest to the time, does not mention it; it was told hundreds of years later.

questions.q: R: How far is it from Marathon to Athens?
questions.a: 40 kilometres

questions.q: R: When were the first modern Olympic Games held, and where?
questions.a: 1896, in Athens.

questions.q: E: Why is the race called the marathon?
questions.a: It followed the route of the legend, from the town of Marathon to Athens.

questions.q: S: Summarise the text in one sentence.
questions.a: A messenger ran to Sparta for help before the battle of Marathon, and a later legend about a run to Athens gave the marathon race its name.

questions.q: P: Which part of the story is history and which is legend? Give one of each.
questions.a: History: the run to Sparta (Herodotus). Legend: the run to Athens and the collapse.

questions.q: Underline the relative clause: The Athenians, who were badly outnumbered, needed help.
questions.a: who were badly outnumbered

questions.q: Add a relative pronoun: Herodotus, ___ wrote closest to the time, does not mention it.
questions.a: who

questions.q: Add brackets for parenthesis: He was a hemerodromos a day-runner trained to run far.
questions.a: He was a hemerodromos (a day-runner) trained to run far.

questions.q: Underline the fronted adverbial: In the summer of 490 BC, a huge army landed.
questions.a: In the summer of 490 BC

questions.q: Write a fronted adverbial of time to start: ___ the Spartans agreed to help.
questions.a: For example: After a long pause, (with a comma)

questions.q: Which punctuation marks the parenthesis here: The runner - tired and thirsty - kept going?
questions.a: dashes

questions.q: Join with a relative clause: The race is 42 km. The race is called the marathon.
questions.a: The race, which is called the marathon, is 42 km.

questions.q: Correct the comma: Exhausted Pheidippides ran back.
questions.a: Exhausted, Pheidippides ran back.

questions.q: Plural of 'city'?
questions.a: cities

questions.q: Add the suffix -ful to 'success'.
questions.a: successful
